newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Indonesia curbs oil product imports from Singapore.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia curbs oil product imports from Singapore.

text.p: Indonesia has curbed its reliance on diesel and jet-kerosene purchases from Singapore by importing more from the Middle East and other regional producers, oil industry sources said on Thursday.
By diversifying its suppliers, Indonesia is aiming for more stable supplies and competitive prices, especially when the market is jolted by emergencies such as refinery problems.

Indonesia started diversifying its supply sources earlier this year and has since reduced diesel imports from Singapore by more than 50 percent and jet-kerosene fuel imports by 20 percent to 50 percent, sources said.

Indonesia buys an average of two million barrels of diesel and up to one million barrels of jet-kerosene fuel a month. In the past it bought most of its supplies from Singapore. Industry sources said Indonesia imported about 70 percent of its diesel from Singapore early last year.
"So far the efforts to diversify have been going on well," one source said. "There are some problems, but nothing major. It's a matter of opening up and providing more alternatives."

Suppliers of Middle East cargoes to Indonesia include Asian and European oil trading firms, as well as Middle Eastern oil companies like Kuwait Petroleum Corp (KPC). Major international oil companies supply most of Indonesia's Singapore imports.

A source with Indonesia's state-owned oil company, Pertamina, told Reuters in April that if the firm's trading affiliates did not have an understanding with major suppliers outside Singapore and Indonesia's demand jumped, they would face rising prices from a limited number of suppliers.

Industry sources said Pertamina decided to diversify its supplies after diesel and jet fuel prices jumped to five-year highs in January and February this year. This was partly due to large purchases by Indonesia itself, after a fire damaged seven storage tanks at the 300,000 barrel per day (bpd) Cilacap refinery in central Java, the nation's biggest refinery.

For November, Pertamina has bought more than four million barrels of diesel due to shutdowns at the Cilacap refinery crude unit between September and early October, and maintenance work at the smaller Balongan refinery in West Java.
Most of the November supplies are from the Middle East, traders said.
Indonesia might still seek more diesel for November, according to sources. Traders estimated November jet-kerosene imports at about 1.5 million barrels.

Sources noted Indonesia's new approach gives it the benefit of acquiring bigger shipments of 60,000 tonnes to 100,000 tonnes each when buying from the Middle East, while Singapore cargoes tend to be 25,000 tonne to 30,000 tonne shipments.
Larger shipments would cut down freight costs because the bigger cargoes are shipped directly to Indonesia, reducing the need to source smaller shipments from four or five terminals.
In the past, Indonesia preferred to rely on Singapore refiners rather than independent oil terminals for its diesel because it was sure of the quality of the product.
"Now that they have taken quite a number of cargoes from other sources, they could feel that diesel from other sources are not that bad after all," one trader said.

But Indonesia's attempts to guard itself against high prices have been somewhat dented by the recent rally in Asian oil prices. Diesel prices climbed to new five-year record highs, trading at $30.55 a barrel in mid-October, while jet fuel has maintained strong levels of around $30.50.
